title: Routing threshold sensitivity and long-context performance matrix
summary: Notes from exploratory profiling across Llama/Mistral/Qwen with MoE routing threshold sweeps on long-context workloads. Focus is on how small gating threshold changes amplify memory and latency variability and which mitigation knobs give the most predictable improvement.
key_findings: Gating threshold (activation clamp / min-score) exhibits non-linear impact on p95/p99 latency for long contexts (>16k) across all three models; Qwen shows the steepest cliff behavior.

Lowering the gate threshold to accept more experts increases parallel fanout and memory working set (KV + activation), which can push certain kernel tilings into a much less efficient path on A100, causing step changes in latency.
Mistral’s FFN I/O patterns make it susceptible to IO-bound stalls when expert fanout increases; the effect shows as throughput cliffs at specific sequence-length × expert-fanout combinations.
Llama variants are more tolerant due to denser attention tiling; their token-forward latency increases more gradually as fanout changes.
Simple microbatching and smaller token fragments reduce p99 variance but at unit-cost regression; adaptive microbatching based on online fanout estimate recovers some efficiency.
A cheap mitigation is dynamic gating clamp (per-request threshold adjustment using recent expert hotness estimate) which avoids extreme fanout spikes for tail requests.
KV cache layout interacts with routing: heavy fanout increases simultaneous KV read bandwidth and causes L2/L3 thrashing on particular GPU architectures, exacerbating p99.
Prefetching the top-k expert KV rows for high-hotness prefixes reduces stall incidence by ~20% in our trials.
Quantization (4-bit) reduces memory pressure but sometimes changes kernel selection and can expose different latency cliffs — must be evaluated together with routing sweeps.
content:
Context:
This doc captures a focused, empirical sweep we ran to understand how routing 'threshold' or min-activation gating parameters affect runtime behavior when serving long-context requests against Llama/Mistral/Qwen model families configured as MoE variants. The objective: identify why small gating changes sometimes produce large p99 regressions and what operational mitigations buy us the best latency stability vs cost trade-off.

Experimental setup (summary):
- Hardware: mixed pool of A100-80GB and H100-80GB nodes; experiments reported are primarily on A100 (unless noted).
- Models: Llama-2-13B-MoE (64 experts, topk=2), Mistral-7B-MoE-like (48 experts, topk=2), Qwen-7B-MoE-prototype (64 experts, topk=2).
- Context lengths: 2k, 8k, 16k, 32k tokens.
- Batch sizes: single-request profiles (B=1) with synthetic concurrency experiments (B=4 microbatches).
- Routing knobs swept: gating_min_score {0.0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.07, 0.12}, gating_temperature {0.8, 1.0, 1.2}.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), GPU kernel time (ms), KV cache read MB, peak GPU memory, throughput (tokens/sec), per-kernel selection map (scheduler logs).
- Tools: our flame capture (flame-runner v2), nvprof-lite traces, kernel-selector logs, and a lightweight runtime hook to capture per-request fanout and expert hit-map.

Observations (detailed):
1) Non-linear latency cliffing (Qwen worst)
   - For Qwen at 16k/32k, moving gating_min_score from 0.03 -> 0.01 increased p99 by 2.5–3x. The median barely moved.
   - Root cause trace: increased simultaneous expert invocations pushed certain attention kernels from a prefetch-friendly tiling path into a fallback kernel with serialized inner loops on A100. Kernel-selector logs showed a jump from kernel-id K_42 -> K_77 at the same sequence length when fanout > ~48.

2) Memory working set amplification
   - More experts accepted => KV cache reads multiply (per-expert KV footprint). At long contexts this crosses the L2/L3 budget and triggers repeated DRAM fetches. Measured KV read MB/request went from ~340MB -> ~1.1GB for Qwen when gate lowered in our 32k runs.

3) Mistral FFN IO sensitivity
   - Mistral experiments show throughput cliffs correlated with FFN staging buffers when expert fanout causes more concurrent FFN calls. This looks like an IO-bound saturation where overlapping FFN launches exceed the kernel fusion planner's sweet spot.

4) Llama resilience
   - Llama-2 variants increased latency more gracefully. Although p99 increases still present, the underlying kernel selector remained on the same high-throughput kernel family until much larger fanout thresholds.

5) Microbatching trade-offs
   - Smaller microbatches reduce peak memory pressure and smooth p99, but they increase per-token compute overhead and reduce peak throughput. Adaptive microbatching (increase microbatch size when observed fanout low, reduce when high) improved p99 tail by ~18% vs static baseline.
next_steps: Prototype dynamic gating clamp: implement a runtime hook that increases gating_min_score by +delta for requests whose recent hotness metric passes threshold.
Add a prefetch path for top-4 experts when long-context and predicted fanout > 32 and measure prefetching overhead vs stall reduction.
Rerun full routing sweep on H100 to see if kernel cliff points shift — capture kernel-selector version and compare.
Add combined quantization + routing sweep (4-bit, NF4-style) to see end-to-end memory/latency surface.
Create an A/B experiment in staging to validate dynamic-clamp on production-like traffic for a limited subset of customers (low-risk routes).
notes:
Quick notes / heuristics observed while poking:
- If you see p99 >> p95 and top-1 kernel time spike, check kernel-selector transitions first. That often explains step-change behavior.
- Fanout hysteresis: small changes in threshold can flip many sequences from single expert -> multi expert, so the distribution is bimodal for tail latency.
- KV layout matters: aligning expert KV rows to contiguous memory for hot experts reduces L2 thrash. We should evaluate re-layout in the data loader.
- Avoid global lower gating_min_score as a default for long-context end-users; prefer per-route or per-request adaptive policies.

Experiment log (short):
- 2025-10-16: initial sweep on A100; saw first Qwen cliff at gating_min_score=0.01, 16k seq.
- 2025-10-20: repeated with pinned kernel-selector; confirmed kernel-id jump correlates with fanout > 48.
- 2025-11-05: added microbatching experiments; adaptive scheme reduces p99 at cost of 6% lower throughput.
- 2025-11-18: prefetch prototype (top-2) reduced stalls but increased average memory by ~150MB; net p99 improvement ~12%.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why does kernel-selector choose the fallback kernel at a particular fanout boundary? Need to inspect the selector heuristics and cost model.
- How does GPU PCIe topology and multi-GPU spans (model parallel shards) change the cliff points? Our single-GPU tests are indicative but not complete.
- Could a smarter KV layout or compression reduce the effective L2 pressure enough to avoid kernel fallback?

Immediate action items (owners):
- Priya: spike on dynamic gating clamp prototype (WIP).
- Ethan: dig into kernel-selector heuristics and add more verbose logging for the selection decision (RD-4123).
- Marco: run a controlled H100 sweep and collect per-kernel runtime counts.
- Leah: prototype expert-KV prefetch indices and measure memory overhead.
